title: Paul in Athens (Acts 17:16–34)
hook: he quotes their own poets: in him we live and move and have our being

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lydia and the jailer, and two men singing in the stocks. Your line was sing at midnight. What did you hum in a dark moment? Day eighty-five.

Think of the last time you talked with someone who sees the world very differently from you. At a wedding, maybe, or in a comment thread. Where did you start? Most of us start with where they're wrong. Now go to Athens, the most famous city of ideas in the ancient world. Paul is there alone, waiting for his friends. He walks the streets, and he's deeply stirred: the city is full of statues and altars to many gods, and he's a Jew who worships one. He talks in the synagogue, and in the marketplace with anyone who'll listen, including philosophers from two big schools, the Stoics and the Epicureans. Some call him a babbler. Others are curious. So they bring him up to the Areopagus, the hill where the city's council met, and say: tell us this new thing.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `A CITY OF IDEAS.` → `UP TO THE AREOPAGUS.`

segments.voice: Paul begins, surprisingly, with a compliment. I see you're a very religious people, he says. Walking around, I found an altar with this inscription, in the King James Bible: "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD." He doesn't mock it. He starts from it. The one you honor without knowing, he says, that's the one I'm telling you about: the God who made the world, who doesn't live in buildings made by hands, and who isn't far from any of us. And then he does something no one expects from a traveling Jewish teacher. He quotes their own poets: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." The second line comes from Aratus, a Greek poet who lived about three centuries earlier. The first is often credited to another old Greek poet, Epimenides, though scholars aren't sure. Either way, Paul stands on their hill and speaks their language, quoting the books on their shelves. Then he gets to his own center: a day of judgment, and a man raised from the dead. That's where the room splits. When they hear about resurrection, some laugh at him. Others say, politely, we'll hear you again about this. And a few believe, and Luke names two: Dionysius, a member of the council, and a woman named Damaris. Christians have pointed to this speech for centuries as a way to talk across a gap: start with what's good and true in the other person's world, honor it, and then say plainly what you believe. And a line Paul borrowed from Greek poets has been said in Christian prayers and sung in hymns ever since. In him we live.
screen: `TO THE UNKNOWN GOD.` · `HE STARTS FROM WHAT THEY HAVE.` · `QUOTING THEIR OWN POETS.` · `SOME LAUGH. SOME STAY.` · then, large: `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one good thing in a stranger's view. Sit, and breathe. Think of a view you don't share. A politics, a faith, a way of raising kids, a way of spending money. Picture someone who holds it. Now look for their altar to the unknown god: the thing they're reaching for that you can honor. Safety, maybe. Fairness. Freedom. Love for their family. Name it to yourself, kindly. You don't have to agree with them. Just find the good. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Paul in Athens. An altar to an unknown god, two lines from Greek poets, and a speech that began with a compliment.
Your line: in him we live. Today, in one disagreement, name something true on the other side before you say anything else. Tomorrow, two weeks of storm at sea. Day eighty-five.

howItsDone: Christians often point to Paul's speech on the Areopagus as a model for speaking respectfully with people of other views. The line 'in him we live, and move, and have our being' is widely used in prayers and hymns.

original.note: Greek: to an unknown god, the inscription Paul read on an altar in Athens.

trapdoor: what you thought: in him we live is a Bible verse.
what it means: it is, and Paul is quoting Greek poets to Greek listeners, starting from what's true in their world.
what a scholar hears: we are his offspring is from Aratus's Phaenomena; in him we live is often credited to Epimenides, but that attribution is uncertain.

sources.quoted: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.

notes: Acts 17:22: the KJV reads 'too superstitious'; the Greek deisidaimonesterous can mean 'very religious'. The script paraphrases as 'very religious' without quoting the KJV. Confirm.
Aratus (c. 315–240 BC) said to have lived 'about three centuries earlier'; confirm.
The attribution of 'in him we live' to Epimenides is traditional (via later Christian commentators) and uncertain; the script says so.
Areopagus: both the hill and the council that met there; the script says 'the hill where the city's council met'. Confirm.
Paul's being 'stirred' by the images is described from Acts 17:16 without judging Greek religion; confirm tone.

Audit (second sample): the unsourced superlative that the line 'became one of the most loved in the whole New Testament' is now the narrower claim that it has been used in Christian prayers and hymns ever since (which howItsDone already says).
